# Add `jig github setup` and a manual-dispatch workflow for personal repositories

One part of the GitHub Actions workflow work. **Treat this request as self-contained**: everything needed is below. Don't assume access to any other issue or to `docs/specs/github-actions-workflow.md`.

## What

A new command writes a GitHub Actions workflow into the target repository for the operator to review and commit. With it, the operator starts `jig github implement` for an issue by hand from the Actions tab. The workflow installs a pinned jig release from the package registry, runs on a Docker-capable runner and acts as a GitHub App. New documentation walks through setup on a personal GitHub account, with no organization, paid plan or hosted service.

## Why

Without a workflow and setup steps, `jig github implement` only runs from someone's laptop. Each repository has to be able to use it without a checkout of jig's source, and jig's own repository is just the first one.

## Context

jig is a Node CLI (TypeScript, Vitest) that turns a markdown request into planned slices, has one agent implement and another review each slice inside a Docker sandbox, and lands them on one run branch, `jig/run/<id>`. Before editing, read `README.md`, `docs/architecture.html`, `CLAUDE.md`, and every `.claude/rules/` file that covers a file you will change, specs included.

The layering is domain rules (`src/domain/`) → flows and steps (`src/flow/`, `src/steps/`) → ports (`src/ports/`) → adapters (`src/adapters/`). Composition lives in `src/app/` and commands in `src/cli/`. Specs sit beside the code as `*.spec.ts` and pass fakes for ports, never module mocks. Anything that touches git is tested against a real temporary repository (`tests/support/temp-repo.ts`).

This issue is one part of the GitHub Actions workflow. In that workflow an operator marks GitHub issues ready, and jig, running in GitHub Actions under a GitHub App identity, implements them, opens PRs and works on review feedback. The jig core, called the *execution engine* (plan, implement, verify, review), stays independent of GitHub. The GitHub code is an *integration*: optional, jig-owned code in its own directory (`src/integrations/github/` unless one already exists). It depends on core contracts, and the core never imports it. jig must start without the integration or its credentials.

- `jig github implement --issue <n>` exists and publishes PRs, draft PRs and comments.
- `jig init` already writes files for the operator to review and commit (`.sandcastle/Dockerfile`, `jig.config.json`); follow its pattern. Nothing else in the target's tracked files may change.
- Releases are published to GitHub Packages by `.github/workflows/publish.yml`.
- `docs/authentication.md` covers agent credentials, including the Codex login cache that jig writes back.

## Recorded operator decisions

These decisions settle the authentication ambiguity that blocked saved run `add-jig-github-setup-and-a-manual-89ca2c32` at design-review finding F2. They are part of this request, not an instruction to skip design review.

- Use one dedicated GitHub App per target repository for this version. Create/install it only for that repository; configure its identity and private key in that repository's Actions configuration/secrets. Mint installation tokens explicitly scoped to that repository. No shared multi-repository App, central service, automatic App provisioning, or workflow-write permission is required.
- Existing agent-provider authentication is authorized inside the sandbox, limited to the allowlist under **Don't undo these**. GitHub authentication is excluded from that allowlist and stays host-only.
- Authenticate both host Git transport and GitHub API operations using the repository-scoped App identity. Passing a token only to Octokit is insufficient when checkout credential persistence is disabled. Include receipt/state fetches and pushes as well as run-branch publication. Use ephemeral host-only authentication without writing credentials to files or exposing them in command arguments, remote URLs, logs or sandbox inputs.

### Flow examples

```text
Configure repository A's dedicated App and selected provider authentication
Dispatch A's workflow for an issue
  -> host mints an installation token scoped to A
  -> host authenticates Git remote operations and GitHub API publication
  -> sandbox receives only the selected agents' allowlisted provider authentication
  -> agents implement inside the sandbox
  -> host publishes the branch and PR; a person reviews and merges
  -> uploaded logs contain neither GitHub nor provider credential values
```

```text
Choose supported Codex login-cache authentication
  -> use the established explicitly selected private cache copy
  -> permit valid refreshed credentials to be written back under the existing contract
  -> never include that cache in target context, generated workflow content, images or artifacts
  -> document provisioning and writeback limitations on ephemeral Actions runners
```

```text
Set up repository B
  -> configure B's own App and secrets
  -> A's GitHub credentials are never supplied to B or to either sandbox
```

## Target

- **`jig github setup`** writes the workflow from a versioned template that ships in the package. The generated file records its template version. jig refuses, with a clear message, a workflow whose template version it does not support.
- **The workflow** only maps the trigger (`workflow_dispatch` with an issue number) to the command and passes credentials. It runs from the default branch, installs the pinned jig version from the registry (never jig code from a checkout), mints a repository-scoped installation token with `actions/create-github-app-token`, and uploads jig's logs as an Actions artifact.
- **Trusted inputs:** the job takes `jig.config.json` and `.sandcastle/Dockerfile` from the default-branch commit it checked out, records that commit (the *trusted commit*) in the request, and uses it for the whole execution. The image build gets no credentials, and its build context holds only content from that commit.
- **`docs/github.md`**, linked from `docs/README.md`, covers:
  - creating the App on a personal account and its permissions: contents, pull requests and issues, never workflows
  - secrets
  - how the workflow authenticates to the registry for the pinned package
  - which agent login modes work on a runner that keeps no files between jobs, saying whether the Codex login cache works
  - Docker on the runner
  - runner and provider costs, kept separate from the fact that no paid plan is needed
  - upgrading the template and the pinned jig version
  - that installing the App alone sets up nothing

## Don't undo these

- **Agents and project commands run only inside the sandbox.** Never on the runner host, not even "for CI".
- **GitHub credentials stay host-only.** The GitHub App private key, installation/publishing tokens, and Git transport authentication must never enter sandbox environments, mounts, files, image/build inputs, prompts, logs or uploaded artifacts. Only host orchestration and publication may use them.
- **Agent credentials are explicitly allowlisted.** Retain jig's existing supported provider authentication for the selected agents: provider credentials injected as runtime environment variables and the documented private copy of an explicitly selected Codex login cache, including valid refresh writeback. This exception permits those agent credentials inside the sandbox; it does not permit unrelated host credentials, bulk environment forwarding, or GitHub credentials. Keep provider values out of prompts, logs, reports, images/build inputs and uploaded artifacts. Preserve the existing documented operator-approved `.jig/.env` behavior and private Codex-cache protections; do not introduce additional credential files or authentication mechanisms.
- **The core never imports the GitHub integration.** Dependencies point from the integration toward core contracts.
- **The host publishes, not the sandbox.** Pushes, PRs and comments are made by the GitHub integration in the host process.
- **No automatic merge.** A person merges every PR. `mergeMode` does not apply to runs this automation starts.

## Done when

- [ ] Boundary specs with sentinel credentials prove selected provider authentication remains usable through supported sandbox paths while GitHub credentials never reach sandbox/build inputs, prompts, files, logs or uploaded artifacts. Do not claim provider authentication is credential-free.
- [ ] Host Git and API publication both authenticate with the selected repository App when checkout credential persistence is disabled; permission scope and credential-free failure diagnostics are covered.

- [ ] Specs: setup writes the workflow with its template version; an unsupported version is refused; no other tracked file changes
- [ ] Opt-in live check, run by hand and described in `docs/testing.md`: in a disposable personal repository without jig's source, dispatching the workflow for an issue opens a PR, and the repository's ordinary CI runs on that PR
- [ ] `npm run validate` passes from the repository root



Source: https://github.com/ygrishajev/jig/issues/15

# Design

## Goal

Add `jig github setup` to generate a reviewable, versioned workflow that manually implements a GitHub issue using a published jig release and a dedicated repository GitHub App. Preserve sandbox-only execution, host-only GitHub authentication and publication, supported provider authentication, and human merging.

## Context

The optional GitHub integration lives in `src/integrations/github/`. Its CLI currently supplies `GITHUB_TOKEN` or `GH_TOKEN` to Octokit, while orchestration refs, execution-state storage, and branch publication rely on ambient Git authentication through `src/adapters/git/remote-ref.ts`. Git errors can include raw stderr.

`implement-issue.ts` enforces default-branch execution, snapshots the issue, disables merging, and defers publication to the host. Request snapshots do not yet record a trusted commit. Configuration and sandbox image construction currently read the working checkout rather than immutable committed inputs.

`src/app/init-sandbox.ts` provides the guarded-write precedent. Package builds currently compile TypeScript and ship `dist` and `presets`, so template distribution needs explicit handling. The actual release channel is public npm, contrary to the request's GitHub Packages statement.

Selected provider credentials and explicitly selected private Codex-cache copies are supported sandbox authentication paths. Additional `.sandcastle/.env` injection and broad telemetry forwarding need tightening.

Before implementation, read README, CLAUDE.md, the architecture map, and applicable house rules, including rules covering specs. Keep integration dependencies directed toward core contracts. Use typed expected failures, adjacent behavior specs, port fakes, setup functions, and real temporary repositories for Git behavior.

## Chosen approach

### Setup and template ownership

Keep setup, workflow compatibility, bootstrap policy, and GitHub execution policy in the integration. Ship a versioned template directory explicitly included in the npm package and resolve it relative to the installed package. Use a YAML library to inspect metadata and workflow structure.

`jig github setup [--jig-version <version>] [--upgrade]` writes only `.github/workflows/jig-implement.yml`. Default to the installed package's exact release version. Development builds require an explicit stable release version; reject ranges, tags, and the development placeholder. Validate explicit pins against public npm metadata before writing.

The workflow records its template version and supplies it to both bootstrap and implement. Both commands reject unsupported versions before authentication or execution side effects, with a typed error identifying supported versions.

Create absent workflows exclusively after ancestor/file symlink checks. Identical output is a no-op. Preserve different existing content unless `--upgrade` requests replacement and its template version is supported. Refuse unknown, missing, or malformed markers even during upgrade; document manual review and replacement. Use atomic replacement with a concurrent-change check. Do not commit, edit ignores or configuration, or modify other tracked files.

### Thin manual workflow and credential-free checkout storage

Declare only `workflow_dispatch`, with a required issue number, and reject dispatches outside the repository's default branch. Pass event-derived values through environment variables and quoted arguments rather than interpolating them into shell code.

Use a Docker-capable Linux runner and a pinned compatible Node setup action. Install the exact published `@ygrishajev/jig` release from public npm before fetching the target repository. Installation requires no registry token, source build, target dependency installation, or target scripts. Pin action revisions during implementation.

Mint an installation token with `actions/create-github-app-token`, explicitly supplying the current owner, the single current repository name, and contents, pull-requests, and issues write permissions. Use a repository variable for the App ID and a repository secret for its private key. Keep built-in workflow-token permissions minimal. The private key is available only to the minting action; the installation token is available only to packaged host bootstrap and orchestration. No workflows permission is requested.

Do not use `actions/checkout` for this workflow. `persist-credentials: false` does not establish that authentication was never written to disk. Instead add `jig github bootstrap --repository <owner/name> --destination <path> --workflow-template-version <version>` to the packaged integration. It runs without target configuration or Docker and uses the same repository-scoped host authentication contract as implement.

Bootstrap validates token scope and repository identity, obtains the default branch through the authenticated API, initializes an empty repository at an absent or empty destination, configures only a credential-free canonical remote URL, and fetches the default branch with full history using child-process environment authentication. Resolve the fetched branch tip once, check out that exact commit on the default branch without executing repository hooks or filters, and return its SHA through a defined machine-readable result. Only the nonsecret SHA is written to the Actions output channel. Reject symlink destinations, nonempty destinations, and identity mismatches rather than overwriting existing content.

The workflow invokes bootstrap into a dedicated workspace subdirectory, then invokes implement there with that SHA as `--trusted-commit` and the template version. The installed package owns all authenticated fetch and checkout behavior; workflow shell remains a thin adapter. Initial fetch, subsequent receipt/state operations, and publication all share the no-credential-files requirement.

Bound the job to 45 minutes because installation tokens expire after one hour. Document that this bounds execution rather than guaranteeing completion. Use non-cancelling issue-level concurrency, preserve normal token revocation, and attempt sanitized-log upload on success or failure when runner teardown permits. Renewable multi-hour execution is outside this version.

### One host authentication scope

Introduce a GitHub-neutral host remote-operation contract, supplied through composition. It covers bootstrap's initial fetch, repository discovery requiring remote access, receipt and lease operations, execution-state fetches and pushes, and run-branch publication. The integration constructs it from the same token used by Octokit.

Validate canonical HTTPS repository destinations and reject mismatched fetch/push URLs, credential-bearing URLs, unsupported transports, and redirects. Supply a repository-specific HTTP authorization header using child-process `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`, `GIT_CONFIG_KEY_*`, and `GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_*` environment entries. Credentials and their encodings must never occur in arguments, remote URLs, Git configuration files, temporary credential files, diagnostics, or global process environment.

Use a controlled Git configuration and child environment that disables credential helpers, prompts, inherited authentication headers, URL rewriting, tracing, hooks, and external filters for bootstrap and authenticated operations. Do not inherit ambient authentication or fall back to another identity. Nonsecret Git metadata and ordinary checked-out content may be written normally.

Inspect installation-token repository access before bootstrap fetch or execution and require exactly the selected repository. Explicitly request the three write permissions in the token action. Convert API and Git permission, expiry, and transport failures into actionable sanitized typed errors without response-object or raw-stderr dumps.

The bootstrap phase is part of boundary verification. Tests must observe files while authentication is active, including repository metadata, home/config locations, and runner temporary directories. Cleanup after an operation is not evidence that credentials were never written. Include partial initialization, fetch failure, and interruption paths.

### Immutable execution inputs

On a new run, require the supplied trusted SHA to equal the default-branch checkout HEAD produced by bootstrap. Persist it in structured request metadata and include it in the request snapshot. A later branch advance does not change the selected commit.

Load existing orchestration state before selecting inputs for a resumed run. Recovery reuses its saved SHA even when a fresh bootstrap checked out a newer default-branch tip; the fresh checkout SHA does not replace the saved run identity. Fetch a missing saved object through the same authenticated host contract if needed, and refuse recovery if it remains unavailable. Reject legacy receipts without trustworthy metadata with recovery guidance.

Add a GitHub-neutral immutable-input contract to application composition. A Git adapter materializes committed blobs in a private temporary directory without checkout hooks or mutable working-tree files. Load `jig.config.json`, presets, and `.sandcastle/Dockerfile` from the trusted source. Preserve the `.sandcastle` build-context convention while including only committed context content. Reject escaping symlinks and credential-file paths; exclude scratch, Git metadata, environment files, and authentication caches.

Build processes receive a minimal environment, no credentials, secret mounts, SSH forwarding, or host credential directories. Freeze parsed configuration for the run and prohibit workflow-mode overrides that bypass the snapshot. Include committed context identity in image caching. Tie the initial execution base to the trusted commit; agent edits to configuration or Dockerfiles affect future runs only. Ordinary core commands retain their existing input mode, and core contracts contain no GitHub policy or imports.

### Credential and output boundaries

Construct sandbox authentication solely from the providers/models selected by frozen configuration. Preserve supported environment credentials and approved `.jig/.env` credential reads with existing precedence. Preserve explicitly selected Codex-cache private copies, source-change checks, validated refresh writeback, and cleanup.

Reject `.sandcastle/.env` injection with migration guidance. Prevent telemetry headers or bulk `OTEL_*` forwarding from becoming additional credential paths. GitHub authentication, host Git environment entries, unrelated provider secrets, and host configuration directories must not enter sandbox environments, clones, mounts, image inputs, or prompts.

Codex login-cache authentication requires an already provisioned, explicitly selected valid cache outside the checkout. A fresh hosted runner has none. Add no secret-to-cache reconstruction, cache artifacts, or automatic persistence. Refresh writeback updates only the selected runner-local source, does not update repository secrets, and disappears with an ephemeral runner.

Sanitize output before it reaches persisted logs, prompts, reports, comments, or errors. Cover known provider values, installation tokens, transport encodings, and streamed chunk boundaries. Bootstrap uses these boundaries before any authenticated operation. Do not rely on Actions masking for artifact-file safety. The App private key remains isolated to the minting action and is never passed to jig.

Export only explicitly selected sanitized log files to the artifact directory. Never recursively upload `.jig` or `.sandcastle`, raw transcripts, state, caches, environment files, or bootstrap temporary directories. Selected provider credentials remain usable through authorized runtime paths; the sandbox is not credential-free.

### Architectural mismatches resolved

Use actual public npm distribution without changing publishing or introducing registry credentials. Replace both action-managed checkout authentication and ambient Git authentication with the packaged, execution-scoped host contract. Select immutable inputs before application/configuration construction. Tighten sandbox injection at its existing owner. Document setup as the narrowly authorized additional target-file write.

## Alternatives considered

1. Passing the App token to `actions/checkout` with persistence disabled: rejected because authentication can still be written temporarily during fetching. Packaged bootstrap owns initial fetch authentication instead.
2. Implementing authenticated checkout and orchestration policy in workflow shell: rejected because it duplicates policy and weakens testability. The workflow calls packaged commands.
3. Using a PAT, built-in workflow token, or ambient Git credentials: rejected because it violates the selected dedicated-App identity or permits API and Git identity divergence.
4. Trusting mutable checkout inputs and warning-only environment injection: rejected because dirty files, agent edits, and additional credentials could influence execution after recording the trusted commit.

## Assumptions

The operator trusts and reviews default-branch workflow, configuration, and Dockerfile content. Each repository has its own App installed only there. Public npm remains the release channel. Provider credentials authorize supported sandbox use. No organization, paid GitHub plan, or hosted jig service is required, although runner and provider usage can incur separate costs. Expiry or permission failure stops safely without identity fallback.

## Non-goals

Automatic App provisioning, shared Apps, multi-repository access, automatic merging or issue triggers, review-feedback automation, registry migration, new provider login mechanisms, Codex-cache artifact persistence, renewable multi-hour execution, and GitHub dependencies in the execution engine.

## Affected areas

GitHub CLI, setup/template assets, bootstrap, request schemas, recovery, authentication, and publication; host Git adapters and remote-store composition; immutable-input contracts and application/image construction; sandbox credential selection and logging/artifact export; package distribution and installed-package smoke coverage; adjacent specs and existing test helpers.

Documentation includes new `docs/github.md`, affected command/authentication/installation/operations/configuration references, `docs/README.md`, `docs/testing.md`, README, target-file exceptions, and architecture descriptions.

# Implementation plan

## Step 1 — Add guarded setup and packaged template compatibility

Read required repository guidance and applicable rules before implementation. Implement setup without opening the execution application, requiring credentials, or invoking Docker. Add packaged template assets, YAML metadata parsing, exact-release pin resolution, guarded creation, idempotency, and supported-version upgrades. Share compatibility validation between bootstrap and implement so both reject unsupported versions before side effects.

Test creation, identical reruns, upgrades, malformed/unknown versions, development-version refusal, unavailable pins, symlinks, concurrent edits, and unrelated-file preservation using real temporary repositories. Build and pack the package, install it in isolation, and generate the workflow outside the source tree. Update setup and upgrade references.

## Step 2 — Implement shared host authentication and packaged bootstrap

Introduce the narrow host authentication contract and sanitized failure handling. Bind the same repository-scoped installation token to Octokit and all Git remote callers, including operations before application startup. Implement child-only environment authentication, canonical destination checks, redirect refusal, controlled Git configuration, and no ambient fallback.

Add the packaged bootstrap command with repository, destination, and template-version inputs. Validate installation scope, discover the default branch, initialize an absent or empty safe destination, add a credential-free remote, fetch full default-branch history, resolve the fetched tip, and check out that exact commit without hooks or external filters. Return the trusted SHA in machine-readable form. Reject unsafe destinations and preserve existing content.

Wire receipt/lease operations, execution-state storage, and branch publication to the same contract. Test with real temporary repositories, a controlled authenticated transport fixture, and GitHub port fakes. Prove initial fetch, receipt/state reads and writes, and publication use the App identity without persisted checkout credentials. Cover extra repository access, mismatched destinations, inherited helpers/headers/rewrites, redirects, expiry, and insufficient permissions.

Observe repository, home/config, and temporary-file writes while authenticated operations are active, including a paused in-flight fetch. Assert neither token nor authorization encoding is written, even transiently. Cover partial initialization, failure, interruption, and cleanup, and assert credential-free diagnostics. Do not treat final filesystem cleanup as sufficient evidence.

## Step 3 — Freeze trusted inputs across execution and recovery

Add trusted-commit parsing and structured request metadata. On new runs, validate the bootstrap SHA against default-branch checkout HEAD before loading configuration. For recovery, load saved metadata first and retain the original trusted SHA despite a newer bootstrap checkout. Retrieve missing saved objects only through authenticated host operations and fail clearly when recovery cannot obtain them.

Add immutable-input contracts, committed-content materialization, and application/configuration/image composition. Keep configuration, presets, build context, and initial run base tied to the trusted commit. Include context identity in image caching and preserve no-merge/deferred-publication behavior.

Test dirty and ignored files, branch movement between bootstrap and execution, recovery after branch movement, agent edits, changed Docker COPY inputs, escaping symlinks, missing objects, legacy receipts, and persisted-state restarts. Assert build inputs come only from the selected commit and builds receive neither host nor provider credentials. Update architecture and recovery references.

## Step 4 — Enforce provider boundaries and sanitized artifact export

Centralize selected-provider allowlisting in the existing sandbox authentication owner. Close `.sandcastle/.env` and broad telemetry injection paths while preserving approved `.jig/.env` credentials and the private Codex-cache lifecycle. Ensure build processes and sandbox clones cannot inherit host Git authentication.

Extend output sanitization to all persistent and prompt/report sinks, including streamed output, and implement narrow sanitized-log export. Use distinct sentinels for installation tokens, authorization encodings, selected and unselected provider secrets, unrelated host secrets, and original/refreshed Codex credentials. Verify workflow wiring keeps the App private key confined to token creation, and use a sentinel to prove it is excluded from bootstrap/implement and downstream inputs.

Exercise successful execution, provider echo, bootstrap/fetch failure, Git/API failure, setup failure, cleanup failure, and streaming boundaries. Inspect environments, mounts, files during execution, image inputs, prompts, logs, reports, and artifacts. Prove selected provider credentials reach supported runtime paths and valid Codex refreshes still write back. Update authentication references.

## Step 5 — Complete and validate the manual-dispatch workflow

Wire default-branch-only dispatch, compatible Node setup, exact public npm installation before target fetching, explicitly repository-scoped App token creation, packaged bootstrap, and implement with the returned trusted SHA and template version. Omit `actions/checkout` entirely. Pass the App key only to token creation, the installation token only to host bootstrap/implement, and selected provider secrets only to implement.

Add the 45-minute job limit, non-cancelling issue-level concurrency, normal token revocation, and always-attempted sanitized-log upload. Pin action revisions after checking their relevant behavior.

findings.concern: The checkout authentication design violates the prohibition on writing GitHub credentials to files.
findings.failureScenario: The generated workflow passes its App installation token to actions/checkout with persist-credentials: false. Checkout still writes the encoded authorization header to a temporary credential file during fetching, then removes it afterward. Thus even a successful dispatch violates the no-file requirement before jig's proposed environment-only authentication contract takes effect.
evidence: The recorded operator decision requires ephemeral host-only authentication 'without writing credentials to files'.
The design explicitly passes the installation token to checkout and relies on persist-credentials: false.

The repository's .github/workflows/publish.yml uses actions/checkout@v7. In [checkout v7's authentication implementation](https://github.com/actions/checkout/blob/v7/src/git-auth-helper.ts), configureAuth invokes configureToken, which writes the authorization value into a RUNNER_TEMP credential file.

In [checkout v7's source provider](https://github.com/actions/checkout/blob/v7/src/git-source-provider.ts), authentication is configured before fetching; persistCredentials=false causes removal in finally rather than preventing the initial write.
findings.recommendation: Specify a checkout/bootstrap path that uses the repository-scoped App token exclusively through child-process environment authentication, including the initial fetch. Keep its implementation in the packaged integration so the workflow stays thin. Extend boundary verification to the checkout phase and inspect temporary files during execution, rather than checking only post-checkout cleanup or rendered YAML.
findings.uncertainty: The design defers choosing exact action revisions. The verified v7 implementation violates the requirement; any alternative revision or action needs explicit evidence that it never writes the credential.

# Design

## Goal

Add `jig github setup` to generate a reviewable, versioned workflow that manually implements a GitHub issue using a published jig release and a dedicated repository GitHub App. Preserve sandbox-only execution, host-only GitHub authentication and publication, supported provider authentication, and human merging.

## Context

The existing implementation owns the requested behavior in these places:

- `src/integrations/github/cli.ts` and `command.ts` register the optional integration. Currently, `github implement` supplies `GITHUB_TOKEN` or `GH_TOKEN` to Octokit but does not bind that identity to Git transport.
- `implement-issue.ts` enforces default-branch execution, snapshots the issue, disables merging, and defers publication to the host. `request-snapshot.ts` currently records issue text and URL without a trusted commit.
- `orchestration-store.ts`, git-remote execution state, and `run-branch-publication.ts` use `src/adapters/git/remote-ref.ts`. Its remote operations inherit ambient authentication, and its errors include raw Git stderr. Publication already refuses workflow-file changes.
- `src/app/init-sandbox.ts` provides the guarded-write precedent. Setup must add one explicitly authorized target-repository write without invoking init or modifying its starter files.
- `src/cli/with-app.ts` loads configuration and presets before execution from the working checkout. `src/app/sandbox-image.ts` builds from the working `.sandcastle` directory. Neither currently provides immutable trusted inputs.
- `config/environment.ts`, Sandcastle agent credential collection, `open-session.ts`, `sandcastle-session.ts`, `private-clone-docker.ts`, and `codex-auth.ts` own credential selection and sandbox lifecycle. Selected providers receive runtime credentials; Codex receives a private copy of an explicitly selected cache with validated refresh writeback. Additional `.sandcastle/.env` injection and broad telemetry forwarding need tightening.
- `package.json` ships `dist` and `presets`; the build only runs TypeScript. `.github/workflows/publish.yml` publishes publicly to npm through semantic-release, contrary to the request's GitHub Packages statement.

The architecture keeps GitHub policy in the integration and dependencies pointing toward core contracts. The five `.claude/rules/` files require cohesive ownership, lifecycle wrappers, typed expected failures, edge parsing, minimal comments, and adjacent behavior specs using setup functions and port fakes. Git tests use real temporary repositories. Public-interface changes require updates across affected existing guides.

## Chosen approach

### Setup and template ownership

Keep setup, workflow compatibility, and GitHub execution policy in `src/integrations/github/`. Introduce a packaged template directory explicitly included in npm's files list, resolved relative to the installed package rather than the current directory. Use a YAML parser to inspect version metadata and workflow structure; do not build a general YAML parser.

`jig github setup [--jig-version <version>] [--upgrade]` writes `.github/workflows/jig-implement.yml`. The default pin is the installed package's exact release version. Development builds require an explicit stable release version; reject ranges, tags, and the development placeholder. Validate an explicit version against public npm metadata before writing.

The workflow carries a template-version marker and passes that version to `github implement --workflow-template-version <version>`. Setup checks existing workflow metadata, and implement checks the supplied version before authentication or execution side effects. Unknown versions produce a typed error naming the version and supported versions.

An absent workflow is created with exclusive creation and ancestor/file symlink checks. An identical generated workflow is a no-op. Existing different content is preserved unless `--upgrade` explicitly requests replacement and the existing template version is supported. Unknown, missing, or malformed markers are refused even with `--upgrade`; recovery is a documented manual review and replacement. Upgrade writes atomically after checking that the inspected file has not changed. No automatic commit, ignore-file edit, configuration edit, or other tracked-file modification occurs.

### Thin manual workflow

The template declares only `workflow_dispatch`, with a required issue number. A job condition rejects dispatches on a ref other than the repository's default branch. The workflow checks out that branch with full history and `persist-credentials: false`, records the actual checked-out SHA, and passes it as `--trusted-commit`. Expressions carrying issue input are passed through environment variables and quoted shell arguments, never interpolated into executable shell text.

Use a Docker-capable Linux runner and an explicitly selected compatible Node release. Install `@ygrishajev/jig@<exact-version>` from public npm without a registry token, source checkout build, target npm install, or target scripts on the host. Resolve and pin action revisions when implementing the template.

Mint the App token using `actions/create-github-app-token`, explicitly supplying the current owner, the single current repository name, and contents, pull-requests, and issues write permissions. The App ID is a repository variable; its private key and selected provider credentials are repository secrets. The private key is available only to the minting action. The installation token is passed only to checkout and host jig orchestration. Do not request workflows permission. Keep the workflow's built-in token permissions minimal.

Installation tokens expire after one hour. Bound this first workflow to a 45-minute job so it never assumes indefinite token validity; document the limit and existing recovery behavior without promising completion of arbitrary-length runs. Upload safe logs on failure as well as success when runner teardown permits, and retain the action's normal token revocation. Supporting renewable multi-hour execution is outside this version. [Token action documentation](https://github.com/actions/create-github-app-token).

### One host authentication scope

Introduce a GitHub-neutral host remote-operation contract, supplied through composition and shared by every remote caller: repository discovery requiring remote access, receipt and lease operations, execution-state fetches and pushes, and run-branch publication. The integration constructs it from the same token used by Octokit.

For GitHub execution, validate the canonical HTTPS repository destination and reject mismatched fetch/push URLs, credential-bearing URLs, unsupported transports, and redirect-based credential forwarding. Supply a repository-specific HTTP authorization header using child-process `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`/`GIT_CONFIG_KEY_*`/`GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_*` environment entries. Disable credential helpers, prompts, inherited authentication headers, URL rewriting, and Git tracing for these operations. The encoded credential exists only in the dedicated Git child's environment, never command arguments, config files, URLs, or global process environment.

Before execution, inspect installation-token repository access and require exactly the selected repository. The workflow requests the three write permissions explicitly; API and Git permission failures become actionable, sanitized typed errors without dumping response objects or raw subprocess details. No fallback to ambient credentials is allowed in this mode. API publication and Git transport must both demonstrably use this scope.

### Immutable execution inputs

The integration selects and validates the initial trusted commit before opening the application. Require the supplied SHA to equal the checkout HEAD on the default branch. The branch may subsequently advance; the recorded SHA remains authoritative.

Persist the SHA in structured request metadata and include it in the request snapshot. Load existing orchestration state before choosing inputs for a resumed run: recovery reuses its saved SHA rather than silently adopting the latest branch. Legacy receipts without trustworthy metadata are refused with recovery guidance rather than guessed.

Add a GitHub-neutral immutable-input contract to application composition. It provides configuration and build-context sources independently of the mutable execution worktree. A Git adapter materializes committed blobs into a private temporary directory, without checkout hooks or mutable working-tree files. Read `jig.config.json` and `.sandcastle/Dockerfile` from this source. Preserve the existing `.sandcastle` build-context convention, but include only committed context content; reject escaping symlinks and credential-file paths, and exclude scratch, Git metadata, environment files, and authentication caches. Build processes receive a minimal environment, no credentials, secret mounts, SSH forwarding, or host credential directories.

Freeze parsed configuration for the run and prohibit config/preset overrides that bypass the trusted snapshot in workflow mode. Include the context identity in image caching so changed committed COPY inputs cannot reuse an unrelated image. Agent changes to configuration or Dockerfiles affect future runs only. Ordinary core commands retain their existing input mode; core contracts contain no GitHub-specific policy or imports.

### Credential and output boundaries

Construct sandbox runtime authentication solely from the providers/models selected by the frozen configuration. Preserve supported environment credentials and operator-approved `.jig/.env` reads, including environment precedence. Preserve the explicitly selected Codex cache's private-copy, source-change checks, validated refresh writeback, and cleanup behavior.

Eliminate `.sandcastle/.env` as an additional injection path and reject its use with migration guidance to supported credential inputs. Prevent telemetry headers or bulk `OTEL_*` forwarding from becoming another credential path. GitHub authentication, host Git environment entries, unrelated provider secrets, and host configuration directories never enter sandbox options, clones, mounts, or build inputs.

Codex login-cache authentication works only when an operator has already provisioned a valid, explicitly selected cache outside the checkout using the established contract. A fresh hosted runner has no such cache. This change adds no secret-to-cache reconstruction mechanism, cache artifact, or automatic persistence. Refresh writeback updates the selected runner-local source; it does not update repository secrets and disappears with an ephemeral runner. Document hosted-runner limitations and dedicated-cache provisioning for suitable runners precisely.

Own credential sanitization at output boundaries before subprocess or agent output reaches persisted logs, prompts, reports, comments, or errors. Cover known provider values, App tokens, and their transport encodings, including streamed chunk boundaries. Do not rely on Actions masking to sanitize artifact files. Export only explicitly selected sanitized log files into an artifact directory; never upload `.jig` or `.sandcastle` recursively, raw agent transcripts, state, caches, or environment files. Secrets remain usable through their authorized runtime paths; the sandbox is not credential-free.

### Architectural mismatches resolved

Use the repository's actual public npm distribution rather than introducing GitHub Packages or registry credentials. Replace ambient Git authentication with an execution-scoped host contract. Move immutable input selection before application/configuration construction instead of patching configuration after startup. Tighten sandbox injection at its existing owner rather than implementing GitHub-only filtering in the workflow. Add the narrowly scoped setup write to the documented target-file exceptions.

## Alternatives considered

1. **Put orchestration and security policy in workflow shell steps.** Rejected because it duplicates integration behavior, leaves local/recovery paths inconsistent, and makes credential boundaries difficult to test. The workflow only adapts dispatch, checkout, credentials, invocation, and artifact upload.
2. **Use checkout-persisted credentials, a PAT, or ambient Git credentials.** Rejected because API and Git identities can diverge, credentials may reach files or clones, and it violates the selected dedicated-App model. Repository-scoped App publication also supports ordinary PR-triggered CI without relying on built-in-token behavior. [GitHub token documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/github_token).
3. **Trust the working checkout and retain warning-only environment injection.** Rejected because local dirt, agent edits, ignored files, and extra credentials could influence builds or execution after the trusted commit was recorded. Immutable inputs and an enforced runtime allowlist make the contract testable.

## Assumptions

- The operator controls and trusts the default-branch workflow, configuration, and Dockerfile, and reviews generated workflow changes before committing.
- Each target repository has its own App, installed only there. App installation alone creates no workflow or provider configuration.
- Public npm remains the supported release channel; this work does not change publishing.
- Provider credentials authorize sandbox use. No organization, paid GitHub plan, or hosted jig service is required, but runner usage and agent-provider usage may incur separate costs.
- The first workflow has a documented execution-duration limit. Credential expiry or permission failure stops safely; neither triggers an identity fallback.

## Non-goals

Automatic App provisioning, shared Apps, multi-repository access, automatic merge, automatic issue triggers, review-feedback automation, registry migration, new provider login mechanisms, persisting Codex caches through artifacts, renewable multi-hour jobs, and changing the execution engine's GitHub independence.

## Affected areas

- GitHub CLI, setup/template assets, request schemas, orchestration recovery, API authentication, and publication.
- Host Git adapters and remote-store composition; immutable-input ports/adapters and application startup/image construction.
- Sandbox credential selection, environment handling, Codex boundary specs, logging and artifact export.
- Package asset distribution and installed-package smoke coverage.
- Adjacent specs and `tests/support/temp-repo.ts`/`fake-github.ts` helpers as needed.
- New `docs/github.md`; affected portions of `docs/README.md`, `docs/commands.md`, `docs/authentication.md`, `docs/installation.md`, `docs/operations.md`, `docs/testing.md`, configuration references, README, house-rule exceptions, and architecture descriptions.
